content: Bibliomania is a type of obsessive-compulsive disorder that involves the excessive collecting or hoarding of books to such an extent that it negatively impacts an individual’s social relationships or physical and mental health. Unlike bibliophily, which is a normal and healthy love for books, bibliomania is a pathological condition. Individuals with bibliomania often collect books that have no practical use to them or lack significant value to genuine book collectors. Common behaviors include purchasing multiple copies of the same book or edition and amassing books far beyond their ability to read, use, or enjoy them. Bibliomania should not be confused with other book-related abnormal behaviors, such as bibliophagy (the act of eating books), bibliokleptomania (compulsive stealing of books), bibliotaphy (burying or hoarding books), or bibliocaust (the destruction of books). Historical Examples of Bibliomania Thomas Phillipps (1792–1872): Phillipps was a British collector who suffered from severe bibliomania. By the time of his death, his collection contained over 160,000 books and manuscripts. His obsession was so extreme that his collection continued to be auctioned off for more than a century after his death. Rev. W. F. Whitcher: An 18th-century Methodist pastor, Whitcher was known for stealing rare books, rebinding them, and then claiming they were rare finds from local booksellers. Fictional Examples of Bibliomania Mel Gibson’s character in Conspiracy Theory: In this film, the protagonist exhibits a form of triggered bibliomania, which is linked to mind control. He compulsively purchases a copy of J.D. Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye every time he leaves his apartment. This behavior is tied to the MK-ULTRA mind control experiments referenced in the National Security Archives. Yomiko Readman in Read or Die (R.O.D): Yomiko, also known as The Paper, is a character in the anime series Read or Die. She works for the British Library and is a bibliomaniac whose apartment is filled from floor to ceiling with books. Unlike most individuals with bibliomania, who typically do not read the books they collect, Yomiko is portrayed as having read thousands of books in her lifetime. Suggested Further Reading Holbrook Jackson’s The Anatomy of Bibliomania (2001) provides an in-depth exploration of the condition and its historical context. Thomas Frognall Dibdin’s Bibliomania: Or Book Madness (1811) is a classic work that examines the phenomenon of obsessive book collecting. Nicholas A. Basbanes’ A Gentle Madness: Bibliophiles, Bibliomanes, and the Eternal Passion for Books (1995) offers a modern perspective on the subject, blending historical accounts with contemporary examples.
